title: Kesar Dairy: Go Direct, or Keep the Distributors Happy?
decision_question: Should Kesar scale its milk-subscription app across Pune, keep it as a small premium channel, or close it?
summary: A farmer-owned dairy cooperative is losing city market share to quick-commerce apps and private brands. A five-month subscription pilot shows loyal customers and valuable data, but delivery costs more than the distributor route and key distributors are threatening to retaliate.

board.name: Ramesh Kulkarni
board.priority: Cash, margins and a payback period the cooperative can afford
board.concern: Delivery cost of ₹7.5 per litre against ₹4.2 through distributors, plus ₹14 crore of investment
board.convinced_by: A credible path to lower delivery cost and a staged investment with clear stop points
offline_questions: Walk me through the unit economics. At ₹7.5 per litre for delivery, where does the money come from?
If we spend ₹14 crore, what is the first milestone at which you would stop?

board.name: Farida Sheikh
board.priority: Protecting the distributor network that delivers 30 years of volume
board.concern: Three large distributors handling 22% of Pune volume may switch shelf space to a rival
board.convinced_by: A plan that protects distributors' earnings or gives them a role in the app
board.lens: Porter: bargaining power of buyers and channel partners
offline_questions: Three distributors carry 22% of our Pune volume. What do you say to them on Monday morning?
How much power do distributors really have here, and how would you reduce it?

board.name: Vitthal Pawar
board.priority: Milk prices and the annual bonus for 42,000 member farmers
board.concern: Money spent on an app is money not paid as bonus, eight months before board elections
board.convinced_by: Clear benefit to farmers: higher volume, a better price, or a protected bonus
board.lens: SWOT: threats to the cooperative and its members
offline_questions: How exactly does a farmer in Satara benefit from an app in Baner?
If the app fails, who pays for it?

board.name: Dr. Meera Iyer
board.priority: Long-term relevance against quick-commerce and private brands
board.concern: Moving too slowly while market share falls from 31% to 26%
board.convinced_by: A sharp view of competitors and how Kesar's data and brand create an advantage
board.lens: Porter: threat of substitutes and new entrants
offline_questions: Quick-commerce takes 12% and delivers in 15 minutes. Why would a customer wait for us until 7 a.m.?
What does Kesar have that a private brand with deeper pockets cannot copy?

title: SkyLane Airways: The Tier-2 Route Bet
decision_question: Should SkyLane put its six new aircraft on tier-2 routes, on existing metro routes, or split them?
summary: A small low-cost airline must deploy six new aircraft. Tier-2 routes have no competition and a subsidy but are below break-even in year 1; metro routes are profitable today but invite fare wars with the two dominant airlines. Pilot shortages and an IPO timeline complicate the choice.

board.name: Anil Batra
board.priority: Margins and cash ahead of the IPO
board.concern: Tier-2 load factor of 68% is below the 74% break-even
board.convinced_by: Numbers showing when tier-2 routes break even and what happens if the subsidy ends
offline_questions: Expected load factor is 68% and break-even is 74%. How do you close that gap?
What happens to these routes in year 4 when the subsidy ends?

board.name: Shalini Gupta
board.priority: Building routes competitors can't easily attack
board.concern: Getting crowded out of metro routes by the two dominant airlines
board.convinced_by: A clear view of competitive dynamics and route-level advantage
board.lens: Porter: industry rivalry and barriers to entry
offline_questions: The two largest airlines hold 81% of metro seats. What happens when we add flights there?
If our tier-2 routes succeed, what stops a big airline from copying them?

board.name: Capt. Harpreet Sandhu
board.concern: 40 captains short, 14% crew attrition, fog and runway limits at tier-2 airports
board.convinced_by: An operational plan that accounts for crew, weather and payload limits
board.lens: SWOT: internal weaknesses and operational threats
offline_questions: We are 40 captains short. Who flies these new routes?
Three airports limit us to 150 passengers in summer. Have you included that in your numbers?

board.name: Rahul Mehta
board.priority: A clean IPO story within two years
board.concern: Visible growth and stable margins
board.convinced_by: A recommendation that tells a growth story without risking margin stability
board.lens: SWOT: opportunities and the investor narrative
offline_questions: How does this decision look in an IPO prospectus?
Which option gives us growth and stable margins at the same time?

title: Mitra Finance: Lending to Gig Workers at Scale
decision_question: Should Mitra sign ZipRide's exclusive lending deal, a narrower deal, or grow without ZipRide?
summary: A mid-sized NBFC can grow its loan book five times through an exclusive deal with a ride platform. The pilot shows strong repeat borrowing but overdue loans above plan, auto-deduction helps but worries riders, and the partner can exit at 90 days' notice.

board.name: Sanjeev Rao
board.priority: Keeping NPAs below 4% so borrowing costs stay at 11.5%
board.concern: Pilot overdues of 6.8% against a planned 4%
board.convinced_by: Risk controls with numbers, and a plan if overdues stay high
board.lens: SWOT: weaknesses and threats to credit quality
offline_questions: Overdues are 6.8% against a 4% plan. Why should we scale that?
What is your stop-loss if overdues stay above 4% after six months?

board.name: Neha Kapoor
board.concern: Losing the deal to a rival lender
board.convinced_by: Terms that protect Mitra if ZipRide changes its mind
board.lens: Porter: bargaining power of the platform as a supplier of customers
offline_questions: ZipRide can exit with 90 days' notice and takes 1.5%. Who holds the power here?
What terms would you negotiate before signing?

board.name: Justice (Retd.) K. Raman
board.priority: Compliance and fair treatment of borrowers
board.concern: Digital lending rules, data consent, and the rider union's complaint about auto-deductions
board.convinced_by: A design that is clearly compliant and fair to riders in a bad week
offline_questions: The union says auto-deductions leave riders with nothing in a bad week. How do you answer that?
How does your plan meet the rules on fees, disbursal and consent?

board.name: Arjun Desai
board.concern: ROE of 11% is low; concentration on one partner
board.convinced_by: A path to higher ROE without betting the company on ZipRide
board.lens: Porter: threat of new entrants and substitutes in gig-worker credit
offline_questions: If this works, what stops other lenders from offering riders the same thing?
What share of our book should depend on one partner?

title: VidyaPath: Should an Online Coaching Brand Open Classrooms?
decision_question: Should VidyaPath open 120 offline centres, franchise to existing coaching institutes, or stay online and cut costs?
summary: An online test-prep company is shrinking as students drift back to physical coaching. A six-centre hybrid pilot shows far better renewals but is below break-even, and star teachers want a bigger share.

board.name: Kavya Rao
board.priority: Cash runway and a route to profit
board.concern: Pilot centres average 180 students against a break-even of 220
board.convinced_by: A phased plan with a stop point if centres miss break-even
offline_questions: Pilot centres average 180 students and break-even is 220. Why open 120 more?
120 centres at ₹1.6 crore is ₹192 crore of our ₹300 crore cash. What happens if they fill slowly?

board.name: Prof. Ravindra Joshi
board.priority: Learning outcomes and keeping star teachers
board.concern: Nine of the top 40 teachers left last year
board.convinced_by: A plan that keeps teachers and lifts the 31% completion rate
offline_questions: Our best teachers are the product. How does your plan stop the next nine from leaving?
Only 31% finish an online course. What does your option do for completion?

board.name: Aditya Malhotra
board.concern: A ₹62 crore loss and shrinking revenue
board.convinced_by: A credible path to break-even without burning most of the cash
board.lens: SWOT: opportunities and the investor story
offline_questions: Which option gets us to profit in 18 months, and how?
If franchising needs no capital, why would we spend ₹1.6 crore a centre?

board.name: Sneha Reddy
board.priority: Winning back students from offline rivals
board.concern: Parents now want classrooms and rivals have already opened centres
board.convinced_by: A clear view of how VidyaPath beats offline rivals, not copies them
board.lens: Porter: rivalry and threat of substitutes
offline_questions: Rivals already have centres. Why would a parent in Kota choose ours?
How does a franchise partner protect the VidyaPath brand if their teaching is poor?

title: Arogya Hospitals: Taking Specialist Care to Tier-3 Towns
decision_question: Should Arogya build 12 small hospitals in tier-3 towns, run existing local hospitals under contract, or stay in its current cities?
summary: A profitable hospital chain wants to reach smaller towns. Building its own hospitals means heavy capital, lower prices, slow government insurance payments and a specialist shortage; an asset-light contract model is cheaper but gives less control over quality.

board.name: Venkatesh Iyer
board.concern: ₹540 crore of spending and scheme payments delayed 110 days
board.convinced_by: Numbers showing the spokes can carry slow-paying patients
offline_questions: Scheme payments arrive after 110 days. How do the spokes pay salaries in the meantime?
Twelve hospitals at ₹45 crore each is ₹540 crore. What's the payback?

board.name: Dr. Farhan Siddiqui
board.concern: Specialists won't move without a 30% premium
board.convinced_by: A staffing and quality plan that works in a small town
offline_questions: Who will be the cardiologist in a 100-bed hospital six hours from Chennai?
Under a contract model, how do we stop a partner hospital cutting corners with our name on it?

board.name: Meenakshi Sundaram
board.concern: 55% of tier-3 patients on scheme rates about 35% below cash rates
board.convinced_by: A payer mix that doesn't depend on the scheme
offline_questions: If the government is the main buyer, who sets our prices?
What happens to margins if scheme rates are cut again?

board.name: Arjun Pillai
board.priority: Getting to smaller towns before rivals
board.concern: Two chains entered tier-2 cities in 2025
board.convinced_by: A clear advantage that rivals can't easily copy
offline_questions: If we wait, what stops a rival chain from taking these towns first?
What does Arogya have in a small town that a local hospital doesn't?

title: Medivance Pharma: Fix, Sell or Pivot the US Business?
decision_question: Should Medivance fix its plant and stay in US generics, sell the US business, or pivot to complex injectables?
summary: A mid-sized drug maker's US generics business is squeezed by price erosion and a regulator's warning letter that has frozen new launches. A buyer has made an offer, the India business is more profitable, and a riskier R&D pivot is on the table.

board.name: Rupal Mehta
board.concern: US margins of 13% against 24% in India
board.convinced_by: A valuation-based case comparing the three options
offline_questions: The buyer offers ₹2,100 crore. What is the US business worth to us if we keep it?
Why spend ₹600 crore on injectables when India earns 24% margins today?

board.name: Dr. Suresh Nair
board.concern: Remediation takes 18 to 24 months with no guarantee
board.convinced_by: A credible remediation plan and honesty about its risk
offline_questions: If clearance fails after 24 months, where does that leave the company?
How do we make sure the data-integrity lapses never happen again?

board.name: Pooja Kothari
board.concern: India grows 11% a year but competes with the US business for money
board.convinced_by: A plan that puts capital where returns are highest
board.lens: Porter: rivalry in Indian branded medicines
offline_questions: Every rupee for Vadodara is a rupee not spent on India. Why is that right?
How do Indian rivals respond if we suddenly have ₹2,100 crore to spend?

board.name: Harish Bhatt
board.priority: Keeping the company large and family-led
board.concern: Selling 46% of revenue shrinks the company
board.convinced_by: Proof that a smaller company is a more valuable one
board.lens: Porter: threat of substitutes and price erosion
offline_questions: Why would we sell half the company my father built?
Prices fall 9% a year in the US. Is that the market's fault or ours?

title: Veloce Motors: Sell the Scooter Without the Battery?
decision_question: Should Veloce adopt battery-as-a-service with a swapping partner, build its own battery plant, or keep selling scooters with batteries?
summary: An electric scooter maker faces a subsidy cut and price-sensitive buyers. Selling scooters without batteries would cut the sticker price sharply but lock it into one swapping partner; building a battery plant cuts costs but needs heavy capital after a safety recall.

board.name: Anjali Deshpande
board.concern: A ₹380 crore plant or a 5-year dependence on one partner
board.convinced_by: A comparison of cash and margins across the three options
offline_questions: The subsidy dropped by ₹5,000. Which option protects our margin best?
What does ₹380 crore of plant spending do to our cash for the next two years?

board.name: Rohit Kulkarni
board.concern: 3,200 scooters recalled after a fire in 2025
board.convinced_by: Control over battery quality, whoever makes it
offline_questions: After a recall of 3,200 scooters, would you hand our batteries to someone else?
If a ChargeHop battery catches fire in a Veloce scooter, whose name is in the news?

board.name: Gurpreet Kaur
board.concern: Dealers earn more on complete scooters
board.convinced_by: A price that sells and a deal dealers will support
board.lens: Porter: bargaining power of buyers and dealers
offline_questions: ₹72,000 sounds cheap, but ₹2,200 a month adds up. How do we explain the real cost?
Why would our dealers push a product they earn less on?

board.name: Vikram Shetty
board.concern: Locking into one partner for 5 years
board.convinced_by: Growth without giving a partner too much power
offline_questions: Who holds the power in a five-year exclusive deal with ChargeHop?
If battery prices fall, which option gains most?

title: Tantu Apparel: Faster Fashion or Slower Craft?
decision_question: Should Tantu speed up to two-week design cycles, move upmarket into certified handloom, or fix its inventory first?
summary: An ethnicwear brand is losing young customers to fast-fashion rivals while sitting on unsold stock. Speeding up means more designs and more inventory risk; going upmarket plays to its weaver network but shrinks its market.

board.name: Sunil Agarwal
board.concern: ₹190 crore of unsold stock and markdowns at 18% of revenue
board.convinced_by: A plan that cuts inventory risk before adding designs
offline_questions: We already have ₹190 crore of unsold stock. How does tripling designs help?
What happens to markdowns if a two-week collection doesn't sell?

board.name: Aarav Jain
board.priority: A brand that young buyers want
board.concern: Only 19% of buyers are under 25
board.convinced_by: A plan that wins younger customers without copying rivals
board.lens: Porter: rivalry and threat of substitutes
offline_questions: A rival launches 40 styles a week at prices 30% lower. Can we beat them at their own game?
What would make a 22-year-old choose Tantu?

board.name: Shabnam Ansari
board.concern: Faster cycles would push work to power looms
board.convinced_by: A plan that keeps weavers' work steady
offline_questions: What happens to our 6,000 weavers in your plan?
If handloom is our strength, why would we walk away from it?

board.name: Deepak Malhotra
board.concern: Stores are slower-moving than online, where customers buy 2.1 times more often
board.convinced_by: A plan that uses stores and online together
offline_questions: Online customers buy 2.1 times more often. What does that mean for our 140 stores?
Will a 25% price rise empty our stores?

title: NetSathi: Wireless Now or Fibre for the Long Run?
decision_question: Should NetSathi reach villages quickly with fixed wireless, build fibre slowly, or do a mix?
summary: A regional internet provider wants to expand into villages. Fixed wireless is cheaper and faster but earns less per customer; fibre lasts decades and earns more but needs heavy borrowing close to its loan limits.

board.name: Manjiri Kulkarni
board.concern: Debt at 3.4 times EBITDA against a limit of 4 times
board.convinced_by: A funding plan that keeps debt below 4 times
offline_questions: Fibre costs ₹610 crore. How do we fund it without breaking our 4 times limit?
How much of the 30% subsidy can we actually count on?

board.name: Rahul Bhonsle
board.concern: Wireless lasts about 7 years against 20 for fibre
board.convinced_by: A plan that doesn't need rebuilding in seven years
board.lens: SWOT: strengths and weaknesses of each technology
offline_questions: Wireless needs replacing in about 7 years. What then?
We'd depend on another operator's towers. What if they raise the 18% share?

board.name: Sarita Yadav
board.concern: A national operator is already offering cheap wireless nearby
board.convinced_by: Speed to market before the national operator arrives
offline_questions: A national operator is already in nearby towns. Can we afford to take four years?
Will a village family pay ₹520 a month for fibre?

board.name: Anand Joshi
board.concern: Monthly churn of 2.8% makes revenue less certain
board.convinced_by: Low churn and conservative borrowing
offline_questions: With churn at 2.8% a month, how sure are you of the revenue that repays our loans?
Which option can you pay back even if growth disappoints?

title: Sthapana Realty: Luxury Towers or Affordable Homes?
decision_question: Should Sthapana build luxury homes, affordable homes, or a mix on its 18-acre Bengaluru land?
summary: A developer with high debt must decide what to build on a large land parcel. Luxury homes earn higher margins but sell slowly; affordable homes sell fast at thin margins. The city already has a large stock of unsold homes.

board.name: Nandini Rao
board.concern: ₹1,100 crore of debt at 12.5% interest
board.convinced_by: A plan where sales cash arrives fast enough to cut debt
offline_questions: Luxury sells 12 homes a month. How long until we sell 900, and what's the interest bill meanwhile?
Which option reduces our ₹1,100 crore debt fastest?

board.name: Kiran Shetty
board.concern: A nearby luxury project has sold only 30%
board.convinced_by: Evidence that buyers will actually come
offline_questions: A competitor 3 km away has sold only 30% of its luxury project. Why will ours sell?
Who buys a ₹55 lakh home here, and can they get a loan?

board.name: Dr. Asha Menon
board.concern: Delivery delays and penalties under the regulator's rules
board.convinced_by: A plan Sthapana can deliver on time
offline_questions: Can we really deliver 3,200 homes in three years on time?
What does the 2028 metro line change about your choice?

board.name: Rajiv Hegde Sr.
board.concern: Affordable homes earn only 14% margins
board.convinced_by: A choice that protects the brand and returns
offline_questions: We are known for quality. Why build at 14% margins?
If prices rise after the metro opens, why sell cheap now?

title: Kinara Hotels: Owning Hotels or Lending the Name?
decision_question: Should Kinara grow through franchised and managed hotels, sell some owned hotels to cut debt, or keep growing by owning?
summary: A hotel chain wants to quadruple its footprint without the debt that owning hotels requires. A franchise pilot grew fast, but guests rated those hotels lower, raising questions about the brand.

board.name: Mohan Krishnan
board.concern: ₹1,700 crore of debt
board.convinced_by: Growth that doesn't add debt
offline_questions: Building one hotel costs ₹180 crore. How many can we afford?
If we sell 5 hotels for ₹900 crore, what do we lose?

board.name: Isha Banerjee
board.concern: Franchise hotels rated 4.1 against 4.5 for owned hotels
board.convinced_by: Real control over quality in franchised hotels
offline_questions: Guests rate franchise hotels 4.1 against 4.5. Why should we put our name on 70 more?
What will you do with a franchise owner who refuses to fix problems?

board.name: Raghav Sinha
board.concern: International chains compete for the same owners
board.convinced_by: Terms that attract owners away from global brands
board.lens: Porter: bargaining power of buyers (hotel owners)
offline_questions: Why would a hotel owner choose Kinara over an international chain?
What does our 1.2 million-member loyalty programme offer an owner?

board.name: Farida Wadia
board.concern: Growing too fast and diluting the brand
board.convinced_by: A pace of growth the brand can carry
offline_questions: Is 100 hotels by 2030 the right target, or just a big number?
How do international chains keep franchise quality high, and can we copy it?

title: ReelDesi: Ads, Bundles or Higher Prices?
decision_question: Should ReelDesi launch a free ad-supported tier, bundle with a telecom operator, or cut content costs?
summary: A regional-language streaming service is losing many subscribers every month while content costs eat most of its revenue. A free tier with ads could grow viewers but cannibalise paying users; a telecom bundle adds volume at a low price.

board.name: Debjani Roy
board.concern: Content costs at 68% of revenue
board.convinced_by: A plan that improves revenue per rupee of content
offline_questions: Content is 68% of revenue. Which option fixes that?
₹45 a month from the operator is less than half our ₹99 price. Why take it?

board.name: Arnab Ghosh
board.concern: Cutting content by 25% would weaken the shows people come for
board.convinced_by: A plan that keeps the original series
offline_questions: Our Bengali originals are why people subscribe. What happens if we cut them?
If national platforms add regional shows, what keeps viewers with us?

board.name: Priyanka Pawar
board.concern: Advertisers pay less for small-town viewers
board.convinced_by: Realistic ad revenue numbers
offline_questions: At ₹140 per 1,000 views, how many views do we need to replace lost subscribers?
What do advertisers want that only ReelDesi can offer?

board.name: Kunal Mitra
board.concern: 11% of subscribers cancel every month
board.convinced_by: A plan that reduces churn, not just adds users
offline_questions: With 11% leaving every month, aren't we filling a leaking bucket?
Who owns the customer in a telecom bundle: us or them?

title: KhetSetu: Should a Farm Marketplace Start Lending?
decision_question: Should KhetSetu offer input credit to farmers through a lending partner, stay a pure marketplace, or pilot credit more slowly?
summary: A farm-inputs marketplace finds that most farmers want credit. A pilot with a lending partner boosted purchases but defaults jumped after a drought. Expanding credit could deepen loyalty or bring losses and reputational risk.

board.name: Rakesh Dubey
board.concern: KhetSetu bears losses up to 5% of loans
board.convinced_by: Clear limits on how much KhetSetu could lose
offline_questions: Defaults reached 9% in the drought district. What's our loss if that happens everywhere?
Credit farmers buy 1.8 times more. Is that worth the risk?

board.name: Sunita Pandey
board.concern: Defaults tripled from 3% to 9% after one drought
board.convinced_by: A plan that handles bad seasons
offline_questions: One drought tripled defaults. What happens in a bad monsoon across all districts?
Why not leave lending to banks who do it for a living?

board.name: Ramesh Yadav
board.concern: Agents collecting debts could lose villagers' trust
board.convinced_by: A plan that keeps agents as helpers, not collectors
offline_questions: Our agents are trusted. What happens to that trust if they chase repayments?
How do we treat a farmer who can't repay after a crop failure?

board.name: Neha Saxena
board.concern: Margins of about 7% on sales are thin
board.convinced_by: A route to higher returns that rivals can't copy
board.lens: Porter: threat of new entrants and substitutes (moneylenders)
offline_questions: Moneylenders charge 3% a month. How do we compete without becoming one?
What stops a big fertiliser company from offering credit directly?

title: SuryaGrid: Sell Solar Panels or Sell Solar Power?
decision_question: Should SuryaGrid move from selling rooftop solar systems to owning them and selling power to small businesses?
summary: A solar installer could switch to owning rooftop plants and selling cheaper power to small factories under 20-year contracts. Returns look attractive, but customers pay late, rules have changed in two states, and the plan needs heavy borrowing.

board.name: Lavanya Krishnan
board.concern: ₹630 crore of investment, with payments already 75 days late
board.convinced_by: A funding and collection plan that holds up
offline_questions: 150 MW at ₹4.2 crore per MW is ₹630 crore. How do we fund it?
MSMEs pay 75 days late today. Why will they pay on time for 20 years?

board.name: Imran Qureshi
board.concern: Installation margins fell from 13% to 9%
board.convinced_by: A model customers will sign quickly
offline_questions: Saving ₹3.2 a unit sounds good. What will make a factory owner sign a 20-year contract?
Rivals are cutting prices. Does this model help us escape that?

board.name: Divya Menon
board.priority: Delivering plants that work for 20 years
board.concern: Owning plants means 20 years of maintenance
board.convinced_by: An operations plan for the full 20 years
offline_questions: If we own the panels, who fixes them for 20 years?
What happens to our panels if a factory closes in year 6?

board.name: Peter D'Souza
board.concern: Rule changes in two states
board.convinced_by: Protection against policy and customer risk
offline_questions: Two states changed the rules in 2025. Which states would you avoid?
What return do you get if defaults double from 3%?

title: Raftaar Logistics: Sell the Trucks?
decision_question: Should Raftaar sell most of its trucks and become an asset-light freight platform, keep its fleet, or run both?
summary: A trucking company with thin margins could sell its trucks and match loads to small fleet owners through an app. The pilot cut costs but on-time delivery fell, and its largest client demands near-perfect timing.

board.name: Rajesh Arora
board.concern: A 5% margin with trucks idle 38% of the time
board.convinced_by: A model that lifts margins without losing revenue
offline_questions: Trucks are idle 38% of the time. Is selling them the only fix?
If we lose the client that is 31% of revenue, what's left?

board.name: Harjeet Singh
board.concern: On-time delivery fell from 94% to 86% in the pilot
board.convinced_by: A plan to get platform trucks above 95% on time
offline_questions: Platform trucks were on time 86% of the time. Our biggest client needs 95%. How?
Damage claims nearly tripled. Who pays?

board.name: Nisha Bajaj
board.concern: The largest client provides 31% of revenue and demands 95% on time
board.convinced_by: A plan the client will accept
offline_questions: What do I tell our biggest client on Monday?
Why not keep our own trucks just for them?

board.name: Col. (Retd.) Vinod Rana
board.priority: Safety and fair treatment of drivers
board.concern: Platform drivers working long hours
board.convinced_by: Rules that keep platform drivers safe
board.lens: Porter: rivalry and bargaining power of suppliers (truck owners)
offline_questions: Rival apps charge owners 7%. Why would they work with us at 9%?
How do we make sure platform drivers aren't driving unsafe hours?

title: Kavach Insurance: Tiny Policies Inside Other Apps?
decision_question: Should Kavach scale embedded micro-insurance through partner apps, renegotiate the partner terms, or limit it to a few products?
summary: A general insurer can sell millions of tiny policies inside travel, shopping and ride apps. Volumes are huge and claims are low, but partners want nearly half the premium and the regulator is watching for mis-selling.

board.name: Srinivas Murthy
board.concern: A 104% combined ratio already
board.convinced_by: Pricing that stays profitable after commission and claims
offline_questions: Claims of 22% plus commission of 45% plus technology. What's left?
Are claims only 22% because customers don't know how to claim?

board.name: Rohan Kapoor
board.concern: Partners hold the customers and want 45%
board.convinced_by: Terms that are fair to both sides
board.lens: Porter: bargaining power of suppliers (partner apps)
offline_questions: Partners want 45% of the premium. Who holds the power here?
What stops a partner from switching to another insurer next year?

board.name: Fatima Shaikh
board.concern: 41% of customers didn't remember buying the cover
board.convinced_by: A design that customers understand and choose
offline_questions: 41% didn't know they bought it. Is that a sale or a trick?
How will a customer know they're covered and how to claim?

board.name: Ajay Menon
board.priority: Customer trust in the Kavach name
board.concern: Small claims often rejected
board.convinced_by: A claims process that works for a ₹49 policy
offline_questions: How does someone claim on a ₹19 trip-delay policy in under five minutes?
What does one viral complaint do to our motor and health business?

title: Pragati Bank: Closing Branches in a Digital Age
decision_question: Should Pragati Bank close its 120 loss-making branches, convert them to small help points, or keep them open?
summary: A private bank does most transactions digitally, but 120 semi-urban branches lose money. They also hold large, low-cost deposits from older customers, employ hundreds of staff and help meet the regulator's rural-presence expectations.

board.name: Gautam Shah
board.concern: ₹132 crore a year to run the 120 branches
board.convinced_by: A plan that cuts cost without losing cheap deposits
offline_questions: If 15% of ₹6,800 crore leaves, what does replacing it cost us?
Do help points at ₹30 lakh a year actually save money?

board.name: Rekha Iyer
board.concern: 58% of these customers are over 55
board.convinced_by: A plan that older customers can live with
offline_questions: 58% of these customers are over 55. What happens to them on the day we close?
Why not make these branches sell more instead of closing them?

board.name: Thomas Varghese
board.concern: The employees' association has asked for no job losses
board.convinced_by: A fair plan for every one of the 900 staff
offline_questions: Where exactly do 900 people go?
What do we say to the employees' association?

board.name: Dr. Vandana Singh
board.concern: Closures in underserved areas draw scrutiny
board.convinced_by: A plan the regulator will see as responsible
offline_questions: How does closing rural branches look against the 25% rural expectation?
If fintech apps already serve these towns, what is our edge?

title: Codeveda: When AI Does the Work You Bill For
decision_question: Should Codeveda switch to outcome-based pricing and retrain staff for AI-assisted delivery, or protect its hourly billing model?
summary: An IT services firm earns most of its money by billing hours. AI coding tools can now do the same work with far fewer hours, and big clients are demanding price cuts. Moving to outcome pricing protects margins but shrinks revenue in the short run.

board.name: Nirmala Srinivasan
board.concern: Revenue down about 12% in the short term
board.convinced_by: A plan that shows when revenue recovers
offline_questions: Revenue falls about 12%. How do we explain that to investors?
Margins rise from 18% to 24% on what volume?

board.name: Suresh Babu
board.concern: Outcome pricing makes estimates harder
board.convinced_by: A way to price outcomes without losing money on overruns
offline_questions: If we promise an outcome and AI doesn't speed things up as expected, who pays?
How do you measure an 'outcome' for a maintenance contract?

board.name: Ayesha Khan
board.concern: Fewer hours could mean fewer jobs
board.convinced_by: A people plan with retraining and fair choices
offline_questions: 35% fewer hours. What happens to the people behind those hours?
Managers are paid on team size. Why would they support this?

board.name: Mark Fernandes
board.concern: Top 5 clients are 41% of revenue and two want 20% cuts
board.convinced_by: A proposal clients would choose over rivals
offline_questions: Two clients want 20% off now. What do we offer them?
Rivals already offer outcome pricing. What makes ours better?

title: FitKul: Gyms, App, or Corporate Wellness?
decision_question: Should FitKul close underperforming gyms and invest in its app and corporate wellness, or keep its gym network?
summary: A gym chain has many loss-making clubs and an app with many downloads but few paying users. Corporate wellness contracts look promising, but moving money from gyms to digital risks the core business.

board.name: Neeraj Gupta
board.concern: Lease penalties on 8 of the 20 gyms
board.convinced_by: A plan that cuts losses net of exit costs
offline_questions: Eight of those leases run for 3 more years. What do the penalties cost?
Only 6% of app users pay. Why put ₹60 crore there?

board.name: Simran Sethi
board.concern: 22,000 members at gyms that would close
board.convinced_by: A plan that keeps members and trainers
offline_questions: Members say our trainers are the best thing about FitKul. What happens to them?
If we keep only 55% of 22,000 members, is that a success?

board.name: Rahul Menon
board.concern: Only 4 companies in the pilot
board.convinced_by: A realistic path to 400 companies
offline_questions: We have 4 companies. How do we get to 400?
34% monthly use: is that good enough for a company to keep paying?

board.name: Ira Bhatnagar
board.concern: Global apps offer similar classes for less
board.convinced_by: A reason customers pick FitKul over global apps
offline_questions: Global apps are cheaper. What does FitKul's app offer that they don't?
Which part of this business could grow ten times?

title: Rasayan Specialty Chemicals: The China+1 Plant
decision_question: Should Rasayan build an ₹850 crore plant backed by a 7-year supply contract, negotiate better terms, or decline?
summary: A global agrochemical company wants an Indian supplier to replace China for a key ingredient. The contract guarantees part of the demand, but Chinese prices have fallen sharply, the plant is costly, and the site faces pollution scrutiny.

board.name: Bhavna Shah
board.concern: Return falls to 9% at the 60% minimum
board.convinced_by: Contract terms that protect returns
offline_questions: At 60% use, the return is 9%. Why build for that?
Our biggest plant cost ₹300 crore. Can we manage ₹850 crore?

board.name: Dr. Kiran Joshi
board.role: Head of Environment, Health and Safety
board.concern: Neighbouring plants fined for effluent discharge
board.convinced_by: A full environmental plan, budgeted
offline_questions: Two neighbours were fined. Why is this site safe for us?
Is the ₹70 crore discharge system in your numbers?

board.name: Rahul Desai
board.concern: Two Indian rivals bidding for China+1 contracts
board.convinced_by: Speed and a strong long-term relationship
board.lens: Porter: rivalry and threat of new entrants
offline_questions: If we say no, a rival signs. What does that cost us long term?
What makes this client stay with us after year 7?

board.name: Prof. Anil Gupta
board.concern: Chinese prices fell 30% in 2025
board.convinced_by: A plan that survives a price war
board.lens: Porter: bargaining power of buyers and substitutes (Chinese supply)
offline_questions: Chinese prices fell 30%. What stops the client switching back after 3 years?
What's the worst case, and can the company survive it?

title: Thali Theory: Leaving the Delivery Apps?
decision_question: Should Thali Theory launch its own ordering app, open dine-in outlets, or cut brands and stay on delivery apps?
summary: A cloud-kitchen company runs many food brands on delivery apps, which take a large commission. It could build its own app, open restaurants, or simplify. Each path has different costs and risks.

board.name: Ashok Menon
board.concern: A ₹28 crore loss with 26% commission
board.convinced_by: The quickest route to profit
offline_questions: 26% commission on ₹380 orders. Which option fixes the economics fastest?
Thirty restaurants at ₹1.2 crore is ₹36 crore. What's the payback?

board.name: Zoya Merchant
board.concern: Only 18% of customers reorder within 30 days
board.convinced_by: A plan that builds loyal customers
offline_questions: Only 18% reorder. Why would they download our app?
71% of orders come from 3 brands. Why keep the other 11?

board.name: Manoj Pillai
board.concern: Restaurants are a very different business
board.convinced_by: A plan the team can actually run
offline_questions: We've never run a dine-in restaurant. Who will?
If we cut 11 brands, how many kitchens can we close?

board.name: Sameer Khanna
board.concern: Delivery apps run competing private-label brands
board.convinced_by: Independence from the delivery apps
board.lens: Porter: bargaining power of buyers (delivery apps) and rivalry
offline_questions: The apps sell their own food brands. Are they our partner or our competitor?
Rivals got about 15% of orders through their own apps. Why will we do better?

title: Dhwani Audio: From Online to Showroom Shelves
decision_question: Should Dhwani Audio enter large electronics retail chains, open its own stores, or stay online?
summary: An online-first earbuds brand is under price pressure on marketplaces and suffers high returns. A large electronics chain offers shelf space, but wants long credit and high margins. Store shoppers spend more, but cash would be tied up.

board.name: Shruti Agarwal
board.concern: 45 days' credit while paying suppliers in 30
board.convinced_by: A cash plan that survives the credit gap
offline_questions: We pay suppliers in 30 days and get paid in 45. Where does that cash come from?
After an 18% retailer margin, what gross margin is left?

board.name: Varun Iyer
board.concern: Margins fell from 38% to 29% online
board.convinced_by: A plan that doesn't start a price conflict between channels
offline_questions: Store prices will be higher. Won't customers check online and buy there?
Returns are 14% online. Is that a channel problem or a product problem?

board.name: Ananya Sen
board.priority: A product people want to try
board.concern: Global brands dominate store shelves
board.convinced_by: Products that stand out next to global brands
offline_questions: On a shelf next to global brands, why does a shopper pick Dhwani?
Store shoppers spend ₹2,900. Do we have products at that price?

board.name: Ramesh Iyengar
board.concern: One chain controls 160 stores and the terms
board.convinced_by: A deal that doesn't make Dhwani depend on one chain
board.lens: Porter: bargaining power of buyers (retail chain)
offline_questions: ElectroBazaar sets the terms. What happens when they ask for more than 18%?
Why own stores at ₹80 lakh each instead of using theirs?

title: Swarnam Jewellers: The Lab-Grown Diamond Question
decision_question: Should Swarnam launch a separate lab-grown diamond brand, sell them in its existing stores, or stay away?
summary: A trusted gold-and-diamond jeweller sees lab-grown diamond prices falling fast and younger buyers interested. A separate brand could capture growth, but could confuse customers and hurt trust in its natural diamonds.

board.name: Leela George
board.concern: Lab-grown prices falling about 25% a year
board.convinced_by: Returns that hold up as prices fall
offline_questions: Margins are 45% today, but prices fall 25% a year. What do margins look like in 3 years?
Why spend ₹220 crore on a new brand if we can use our 62 stores?

board.name: Arun Varghese
board.priority: The right products for younger buyers
board.concern: 61% of under-30s would consider lab-grown
board.convinced_by: A product plan that wins younger buyers
offline_questions: 61% of young buyers are interested. Can we afford to ignore them?
What would a 25-year-old buy from a lab-grown brand?

board.name: Susan Mathew
board.priority: Customer trust and the buyback promise
board.concern: Customers elsewhere couldn't tell natural from lab-grown
board.convinced_by: Clear labelling and honest promises
offline_questions: Our 90% buyback is why people trust us. What do we promise for lab-grown?
How will a customer know for sure what they're buying?

board.name: Joseph Kurian
board.concern: Lab-grown could cheapen the Swarnam name
board.convinced_by: A plan that keeps the Swarnam name premium
board.lens: Porter: threat of substitutes and new entrants
offline_questions: Our grandfather built this name on gold. Do we really want to sell factory diamonds?
Two national brands launched lab-grown lines. Are we late or wise?

title: Jal Seva Foundation: Clean Water After the Grant
decision_question: Should Jal Seva raise water prices, start a paid bottled-water business, or hand its water ATMs to village councils?
summary: A non-profit runs clean-water ATMs in villages, mostly funded by a corporate donor who is cutting support. It must find money without pricing poor families out of clean water.

board.name: Rajendra Singh
board.concern: A 40% cut in grants that cover 70% of costs
board.convinced_by: A plan that covers the gap within a year
offline_questions: Grants cover 70% and are falling 40%. Where does the rest come from?
Bottled water needs ₹18 crore. Where does that come from?

board.name: Kamla Devi
board.priority: Families keeping access to clean water
board.concern: 11% stopped using the ATMs after a ₹1 rise
board.convinced_by: A plan that keeps the poorest families drinking clean water
offline_questions: A ₹1 rise lost 11% of families. What happens at ₹8?
Where do families go if they stop buying our water?

board.name: Vivek Agarwal
board.concern: A model that depends on one donor
board.convinced_by: A path to standing on its own
offline_questions: We can't fund this forever. When does it stand on its own?
Why should another donor fund this if we're cutting back?

board.name: Dr. Nusrat Jahan
board.concern: Some panchayat-run systems broke down within two years
board.convinced_by: A plan that keeps machines working and water safe
offline_questions: Some panchayats let systems break in two years. How do we prevent that?
How will we know if fewer families are drinking clean water?

title: Glowveda: Quick Commerce, Pharmacies or Our Own Store?
decision_question: Should Glowveda shift its ad budget to quick-commerce apps and pharmacies, or keep building its own website?
summary: An Ayurvedic skincare brand sells mostly through marketplaces. Quick-commerce apps are growing fast but take high margins and fees; its own website has loyal repeat buyers but costly customer acquisition.

board.name: Rohit Bansal
board.concern: Quick commerce takes 32% plus fees
board.convinced_by: A channel mix that grows without losses
offline_questions: After 32% margin and listing fees, do we make money on a quick-commerce order?
Pharmacies want 60 days' credit. Can we afford that?

board.name: Tanya Arora
board.concern: Quick commerce growing 9% a month
board.convinced_by: Being where customers are buying now
offline_questions: Quick commerce grows 9% a month. Can we afford to miss it?
What does it cost us if a rival takes the top spot on these apps?

board.name: Dr. Smita Kulkarni
board.concern: Quick-commerce apps launching private-label beauty
board.convinced_by: A plan that builds loyal customers, not one-off buyers
board.lens: Porter: bargaining power of buyers (platforms) and rivalry
offline_questions: The apps sell their own beauty brands. Why help them learn our customers?
Website customers come back 3 times a year. Why not grow that?

board.name: Anil Sharma
board.priority: Company value and the stake offer
board.concern: A larger company wants 30%
board.convinced_by: A strategy that raises the value of the business
offline_questions: A big company wants 30% of us. Does your plan make that stake worth more or less?
Which channel would a buyer value most?
